The Five Good Emperors. Five successive Roman emperors of the second century—Nerva, Trajan, Hadrian, Antoninus Pius, and Marcus Aurelius—reigned during a period considered the zenith of the Roman Empire. Their eighty-four-year period from ninety-six to one hundred eighty A.D. saw territorial expansion, cultural flourishing, legal development, and relative peace and stability, earning them the title Antonine from the dynasty name, and historians regard their era as the high-water mark of Roman civilization before the empire's gradual decline.

Nerva reigned from ninety-six to ninety-eight A.D. and initiated the practice of adopting the most qualified successor rather than hereditary succession, stabilizing the realm after Domitian's tyranny. Trajan reigned from ninety-eight to one hundred seventeen A.D., expanded the empire to its widest territorial extent by conquering Dacia and improving infrastructure, and was celebrated for military prowess and public works. Hadrian reigned from one hundred seventeen to one hundred thirty-eight A.D., consolidated rather than expanded the empire, commissioned monumental building projects like the Pantheon and Hadrian's Wall, and codified Roman law. Antoninus Pius reigned from one hundred thirty-eight to one hundred sixty-one A.D., maintained peace and prosperity with minimal military campaigns, and was known as a restrained, judicious ruler focused on governance. Marcus Aurelius reigned from one hundred sixty-one to one hundred eighty A.D. as the Stoic philosopher-emperor whose Meditations survives, combating plague and barbarian incursions while developing moral philosophy.

This era saw the apex of Roman economic prosperity, architectural achievement, and intellectual culture, with the empire's borders reaching their maximum stability.
